title: Consumer value is being recalculated through AI-mediated discovery, measurable wellness, experiences, and resourceful low-waste spending
source_unit: McKinsey & Company, State of the Consumer 2026: When tech acceleration and cost pressures collide, 22 June 2026
geography: Consumer trends in Brazil, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with global market and category context

observations.period: 2026; consumer sentiment and four trend frame

denominator.unit: consumers surveyed in Brazil, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States

dominant_pressures.value: rapid technology advancement and sustained cost consciousness are identified as broad, persistent forces shaping consumption

trend_set.value: the tech-driven path to purchase, health revolution, experience economy, and resourceful consumer

value_diffusion.value: priority placed on value cuts across income segments and categories while established-channel scale is less decisive

method_context.value: the report combines survey data with ongoing consumer sentiment research and global client work

observations.method: McKinsey consumer survey of 4,863 people in five countries combined with ongoing sentiment research, category analysis, and client-work synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The survey covers five markets and the four-trend frame is an interpretive business synthesis; it is not a representative estimate of all consumers globally or a causal forecast.
observations.subgroup: Consumers across five markets, income groups, generations, health and wellness users, digital shoppers, experience seekers, retailers, brands, and service providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: The prominence of technology and value may reflect the 2026 cost environment and publisher framing; conventional stores, brands, and price sensitivity remain important for many categories and consumers.

observations.period: 2026; AI, social discovery, and purchase journeys

denominator.unit: consumers in the five-country McKinsey survey; generational percentages are reported subgroup shares

gen_ai_shopping.value: 28 percent of Gen Z respondents report using generative-AI tools for shopping versus 16 percent of baby boomers

ai_overview.value: 60 percent of Gen Z respondents report regularly using AI overviews at the top of traditional search platforms versus 29 percent of baby boomers

social_discovery.value: 23 percent of Gen Z respondents report discovering new brands on social media, and 34 percent say social media plays a key role at purchase compared with 16 percent of boomers

information_shift.value: AI-generated answers can reduce clicks to brand, retailer, and publisher sites while making third-party information and signal consistency more important

brand_site_citations.unit: percent of sources cited by large language models in the report's consumer-goods XEO360 data, October 2025-May 2026

observations.method: McKinsey five-country survey, generational subgroup comparisons, and cited XEO360 analysis of sources used in large-language-model brand queries.
observations.uncertainty: The generational comparisons are survey associations, not age effects; XEO360 citation shares depend on query design, model behavior, category, and the measured period, and do not establish consumer conversion.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z, baby boomers, social-media users, AI-shopping users, brands, retailers, publishers, platforms, and creators of third-party product information.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI and social discovery can complement rather than replace stores, search, direct websites, friends, and family; adoption and trust may vary sharply by category and market.

denominator.unit: consumers in the five-country McKinsey survey plus cited external category research

wellness_gap.value: most surveyed consumers say dimensions such as heart health, cognitive function, sleep, stress, and gut health matter, but fewer than half feel they are achieving their wellness goals

health_information.value: 38 percent of Gen Z respondents report turning to social media for health information, while 59 percent of boomers in a cited 2024 McKinsey survey reported turning to doctors
health_information.unit: survey shares from current and cited research

digital_measurement.value: wearables, glucose monitors, and fitness trackers make sleep, glucose, nutrient intake, and heart health more measurable to consumers

food_and_wellness_route.value: consumer demand is moving toward products that reduce trade-offs among taste, price, and health function, with more specific life-stage and physiological segmentation

observations.method: McKinsey consumer survey and synthesis of cited wellness, food-and-beverage, health-information, and GLP-1 evidence.
observations.uncertainty: Several health and GLP-1 figures come from different surveys, dates, and external sources; the report does not establish that wearable feedback or product changes cause durable health improvement.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z, millennials, boomers, wellness consumers, people using wearables or health tools, food and beverage consumers, patients, clinicians, and health-oriented brands.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital measurement can widen attention without improving access, interpretation, or outcomes; health goals and information sources may reflect affordability, clinical availability, and cultural norms.

denominator.unit: consumers in the five-country McKinsey survey, with global market-growth comparisons

experience_growth.unit: percent global experiences-market growth from 2023 to 2025, versus 0.8 percent for nonessential goods

cost_constraint.value: cost remains the most important factor in experience-related purchases even as consumers seek connection, relaxation, excitement, and learning

resourceful_use.value: 82 percent say they use items longer before replacing them, 69 percent repair rather than discard, and 68 percent actively reduce waste

alternative_consumption.value: 30 percent report buying apparel secondhand and nearly half report doing services themselves that they previously paid for

value_recalibration.value: resourcefulness is framed as a broader recalibration of value involving durability, versatility, repairability, resale, and selective splurges rather than uniform withdrawal from consumption

observations.method: McKinsey five-country consumer survey combined with global market-growth comparisons and category examples for experiences, resale, repair, and DIY.
observations.uncertainty: Market-growth figures and survey shares use different populations and measurement periods; reported intentions do not establish actual household budgets, environmental impact, or long-term category performance.
observations.subgroup: Consumers under cost pressure, higher-income selective spenders, Gen Z and boomers, experience providers, resale and repair markets, retailers, and product designers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Resourceful consumption may coexist with higher total consumption elsewhere, and experience growth can be concentrated among consumers with enough income and mobility to participate.

related_sources.claim: McKinsey's ConsumerWise page identifies the report and related consumer-sentiment work.
A related McKinsey chart summarizes the changing relationship among social media, generative AI, and consumer trust.

boundary: This record adds a publisher consumer-research signal about AI-mediated discovery, health and wellness measurement, experience spending, and resourceful consumption under cost pressure. It uses aggregate survey and market synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, a representative global consumer panel, causal health evidence, household budget diaries, or proof that any business response will work.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official McKinsey State of the Consumer 2026 page reviewed for the five-country survey frame, four trends, AI and social discovery, wellness, experience-market growth, repair, reuse, resale, and DIY measures.
